raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were introduced to solve an attractive but difficult problem in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): how to provide transient radial support and antiproliferative drug delivery, then leave behind a vessel free of a permanent metallic cage. The conceptual advantages—restored vasomotion, adaptive remodeling, easier noninvasive imaging, preserved bypass options, and potentially less very late device-related failure—were supported by early ABSORB feasibility studies in selected simple lesions [1,2]. Longer follow-up with computed tomography, intravascular ultrasound, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) suggested late lumen preservation, disappearance of scaffold struts, and recovery of vasomotor function after poly-L-lactic acid resorption [3,4]. These mechanistic observations created strong enthusiasm, but they were generated in small cohorts and under highly controlled implantation conditions.

The first-generation Absorb everolimus-eluting scaffold became the dominant clinical platform. Its limitations were also intrinsic to its design: relatively thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, lower acute radial strength than metallic drug-eluting stents (DES), and a prolonged resorption phase during which malapposition, underexpansion, fracture, or dismantling could become thrombogenic. Subsequent analyses showed that vessel sizing, lesion preparation, and high-pressure post-dilatation were not optional technical refinements but determinants of safety [5,6]. The “PSP” approach—adequate predilatation, appropriate sizing, and post-dilatation—therefore became central to BVS implantation practice.

Randomized trials initially showed noninferiority signals in selected patients. ABSORB II demonstrated broadly similar early clinical outcomes versus cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents, but by 3 years failed its vasomotion and late lumen loss coprimary endpoints and showed numerically more scaffold thrombosis [7,8]. ABSORB III met its 1-year noninferiority endpoint, but 3-year follow-up revealed higher target-lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis, especially in small vessels [9,10]. Pooled ABSORB analyses reinforced that implantation technique and vessel size were major contributors to outcomes [11]. ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan also reported 1-year noninferiority in selected lesions, yet these trials were not powered to exclude uncommon thrombotic hazards [12,13].

The AIDA trial shifted the field by evaluating BVS in routine PCI. Target-vessel failure was not significantly different from metallic DES, but definite or probable device thrombosis was substantially higher with BVS [14]. Large registries similarly reported acceptable procedural success but persistent concern for thrombotic events outside narrowly selected anatomy [15]. Later pooled and long-term analyses clarified the time course: excess risk was concentrated during the first 3 years, broadly corresponding to the scaffold bioresorption interval, and appeared to attenuate thereafter [16,17]. Meta-analyses consistently found higher device thrombosis and myocardial infarction with first-generation Absorb compared with contemporary metallic DES [18-21]. Thus, the technology’s clinical problem was not the bioresorbable concept per se, but the mismatch between early scaffold design, lesion selection, implantation technique, and the very high safety benchmark set by modern DES.

Magnesium-based scaffolds represent an alternative strategy. The DREAMS and Magmaris programs sought faster resorption, improved mechanical behavior, and less chronic polymer burden. BIOSOLVE-I and serial imaging studies established feasibility, and BIOSOLVE-II supported acceptable angiographic and clinical performance in relatively simple de novo lesions [22-25]. The BIOSOLVE-IV registry extended this experience to larger real-world cohorts, showing low but nonzero scaffold-related events when careful lesion selection and implantation principles were applied [26]. These studies are encouraging, but they remain less definitive than the large randomized DES-comparator evidence base available for metallic stents.

Newer polymeric platforms also aim to address Absorb’s shortcomings through thinner struts, improved radiopacity, better expansion latitude, and optimized degradation. The MeRes100, DESolve, and Fantom programs illustrate this direction, with early studies reporting favorable imaging or clinical outcomes in selected lesions [27-30]. However, none has yet demonstrated superiority—or even broad noninferior safety—against current ultrathin metallic DES in large all-comer randomized trials.

At present, BVS should be viewed as an instructive technological cycle rather than a failed idea. First-generation Absorb proved that transient coronary scaffolding is feasible, but also that “disappearing” devices must be at least as safe as permanent DES during the years before they disappear. Future success will require thinner struts, predictable resorption, excellent deliverability, larger expansion windows, imaging-guided implantation, prolonged pharmacologic protection when appropriate, and trials powered for device thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and late clinical benefit. Until such evidence emerges, contemporary metallic DES remain the default PCI platform, while bioresorbable scaffolds remain a promising but selective and investigational strategy.
